title: Names, reserved words, and typed values (identifiers, keywords, literals)
hook: Every line of C# starts with names you choose, words the language reserves, and literal values you type directly. C# is case-sensitive and every statement ends with a semicolon — there is no Automatic Semicolon Insertion (ASI) like JavaScript.

sections.heading: What are identifiers, keywords, and literals?

blocks.text: An **identifier** is a name you give to a variable, method, or type — for example `attemptId` or `ImportRow`. A **keyword** is a word reserved by the language (`if`, `class`, `await`) that you cannot use as an identifier without a special prefix. A **literal** is a value written directly in source code: `199` is an integer literal, `"hello"` is a string literal, `true` is a boolean literal. C# assigns a fixed type to every literal at compile time, so `1.5` is a `double` and `1.5m` is a `decimal`.

entries.plainDefinition: A name you choose for a variable, parameter, method, class, or namespace.
entries.example: string studentName = "Ada"; — studentName is the identifier.

entries.plainDefinition: A word the C# grammar reserves. You cannot use it as an identifier unless you prefix it with @.
entries.example: int @event = 1; — @event is legal because of the @ prefix.

entries.plainDefinition: A value written directly in source code, not computed at run time.
A JavaScript feature that inserts missing semicolons. C# does not have this — every statement must end with ; or use a block structure.
entries.example: Omitting a semicolon in C# is a compile error, not a silent bug.

sections.heading: Why typed literals matter in real code

blocks.text: Choosing the right literal type prevents subtle bugs. Money and grades should use the `decimal` suffix (`199.99m`), not `199.99` which is a `double` with floating-point rounding. Multi-line JSON or Comma-Separated Values (CSV) fixtures in tests are painful with escaped quotes — C# 11 raw string literals solve that cleanly. Comments come in three forms: `//` single-line, `/* */` multi-line, and `///` XML documentation for public APIs.

blocks.title: Unicode and @ prefix
blocks.body: Identifiers can start with Unicode letters, not just ASCII. Prefix a keyword with `@` to use it as a name: `@class` or `@event`. This is common when wrapping JavaScript-style event APIs. The `@` is not part of the runtime name — it is only a compile-time escape.

sections.heading: How the compiler reads your source text

items.title: Scan characters
items.body: The compiler reads your file left to right, skipping whitespace and comments.

items.title: Recognize tokens
items.body: It groups characters into tokens: identifiers, keywords, literals, and operators like + or ==.

items.title: Check keywords vs identifiers
items.body: If a token matches a reserved word, it is a keyword. Otherwise it is an identifier (optionally prefixed with @).

items.title: Assign literal types
items.body: Each numeric or string literal gets a compile-time type based on its suffix and format.

sections.heading: Code walkthrough: names and string literals

snippet.label: Raw string literal for JSON fixtures
snippet.explanation: Raw strings start with at least three double quotes. Use them for EventBridge sample JSON, CSV headers, or any multi-line text. For interpolation, prefix with $: $"""count={n}""".

snippet.label: Literal kinds and their types
snippet.code:
int count = 199;           // int
long big = 199L;           // long
int hex = 0xFF;            // hex int
int binary = 0b1010;       // binary int
double ratio = 1.5;        // double — not for money!
decimal price = 1.5m;      // decimal — use for money
char letter = 'A';         // char (single quotes)
string name = "Ada";       // string
int readable = 1_000;      // digit separators OK
snippet.explanation: The suffix matters: L for long, m for decimal, f for float. Without a suffix, 1.5 is double. Money and grades should use decimal (m), not double.

snippet.label: @ prefix and contextual keywords
snippet.explanation: @ escapes any keyword to use it as an identifier. Contextual keywords like var, from, and yield are only reserved in specific grammar positions.

blocks.title: C# vs JavaScript/TypeScript literals
rows: int, long, decimal, double — chosen by suffix
Inferred static type at compile time

blocks.title: Top pitfalls
blocks.body: Using 1.5 (double) for money when you need 1.5m (decimal). Fighting JSON braces inside $"..." interpolation — switch to $""" raw interpolation. Treating var as dynamic — it is compile-time type inference, not runtime typing. Forgetting semicolons after expecting JavaScript Automatic Semicolon Insertion (ASI).

interviewTakeaways: C# has no Automatic Semicolon Insertion (ASI); every statement ends with ; or uses a block.
Raw string literals (C# 11) are the default answer for multi-line JSON or CSV in source.
The @ prefix lets you use a keyword as an identifier; it does not change the runtime name.
Literal suffixes (m, L, f) determine the compile-time type — choose decimal for money.
commonPitfalls: Using 1.5 (double) for money literals — you wanted 1.5m (decimal).
Interpolating JSON with $"{ ... }" and fighting braces; use $""" raw interpolation.
Treating var as a keyword that makes the variable dynamic — it is inferred static type.
Expecting JavaScript-style truthy checks on numbers in if conditions — C# requires bool.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript Automatic Semicolon Insertion (ASI) and template strings (backticks) are the closest analog to C# semicolons and $""" raw interpolated strings, but C# interpolation is typed at compile time.
